metadata.title: Characteristics of the schools resilient to violence. A study based on data from ICCS 2016 in Chile, Mexico and Colombia

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses ICCS 2016 microdata and restricts the analytic sample to high-risk schools in Chile, Mexico, and Colombia, defined using principals’ perceptions of crime in the community (C_COMCRI). Because the authors analyze school-level resilience using aggregated student and school variables, they explicitly state that they account for ICCS’s complex sampling and assessment design by applying sampling weights to adjust for disproportional subgroup sampling and nonresponse. They also apply replicate weights to account for the nested structure of the data, following ICCS technical guidance (Schulz et al., 2018). The paper does not report a specific weight variable name (e.g., W_FSTUWT), but it clearly indicates both sampling and replicate weights were used in the estimation procedures.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper uses ICCS-derived civic knowledge with PV notation (e.g., PV1CIVm), implying plausible values were incorporated, but it does not describe how missing data were handled (e.g., whether cases with missing questionnaire items were excluded or imputed). This is a reporting gap because missingness is common in large-scale assessments and the choice of missing-data strategy can affect both CART variable importance and logistic regression coefficients.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: ICCS 2016 (8th graders) was restricted to a subset of schools identified as ‘high-risk’ in Chile, Mexico, and Colombia. High-risk schools were defined as those with principals’ perceptions of crime in the community (C_COMCRI) scores higher than the national average; only these high-risk schools were included. The dependent variable ‘Resilient to Violence’ was constructed at the school level: schools with high community violence risk (C_COMCRI above national mean) and low incidence of violence (students’ experiences of physical and verbal abuse at school, S_ABUSE, below national mean). Student-level questionnaire variables were aggregated to the school level by taking mean values across students attending each school, and the analysis used a total of 84 independent variables (derived school variables plus derived student variables; scales used to construct the outcome were excluded to avoid duplication).

Willingness to participate in school activities

main_findings.dataset_used: ICCS 2016 Grade 8 (Civics and Citizenship) — Chile high-risk schools subset
main_findings.performance_metrics: Logistic regression (Chile): Nagelkerke R2 = 0.46 (Cox & Snell R2 = 0.34); N = 2581. CART: 16 variables retained above 40% normalized importance (tree-based importance ranking; no single accuracy metric reported).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS 2016 Grade 8 data for Chile high-risk schools, the study leveraged student interaction quality (S_INTACTm), openness in classroom discussions (S_OPDISCm), acceptance of neighborhood diversity (L_ATTDIVm), civic knowledge (PV1CIVm), and endorsement of violence (L_ATTVIOLm) to predict whether a school was resilient to violence, finding that more positive interaction and openness were associated with higher resilience while greater endorsement of violence was associated with lower resilience. This indicates that strengthening classroom interaction climate and civic-oriented attitudes may be a practical route to improving school safety, though the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICCS 2016 Grade 8 (Civics and Citizenship) — Mexico high-risk schools subset
main_findings.performance_metrics: Logistic regression (Mexico): Nagelkerke R2 = 0.56 (Cox & Snell R2 = 0.40); N = 3488. CART: 16 variables retained above 40% normalized importance (tree-based importance ranking; no single accuracy metric reported).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS 2016 Grade 8 data for Mexico high-risk schools, the study leveraged student interaction quality (S_INTACTm), importance of social-movement related citizenship (S_CITSOCm), participation at school (S_SCHPARTm), empathy toward classmates (L_EMPCLASm), and endorsement of violence (L_ATTVIOLm) to predict school resilience to violence, finding that more positive interaction and empathy were associated with higher resilience while higher participation measures were associated with lower resilience and the direction of some attitude variables was counterintuitive. This indicates that interventions should focus on the quality and structure of student engagement and prosocial civic attitudes rather than assuming that participation alone will reduce violence.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICCS 2016 Grade 8 (Civics and Citizenship) — Colombia high-risk schools subset
main_findings.performance_metrics: Logistic regression (Colombia): Nagelkerke R2 = 0.34 (Cox & Snell R2 = 0.25); N = 3185. CART: variables retained above 40% normalized importance (no single accuracy metric reported).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS 2016 Grade 8 data for Colombia high-risk schools, the study leveraged endorsement of gender equality (S_GENEQLm), student interaction quality (S_INTACTm), empathy toward classmates (L_EMPCLASm), personal responsibility for citizenship (S_CITRESPm), and endorsement of violence (L_ATTVIOLm) to predict school resilience to violence, finding that prosocial civic attitudes and empathy were associated with higher resilience while some participation-related and classroom openness variables showed negative associations and endorsement of violence showed a positive association. This indicates that resilience-building policies may need to prioritize empathy and equality-oriented civic responsibility while carefully designing participatory practices to avoid unintended effects.

data.outcome_summary: This study uses ICCS 2016 Grade 8 data for a high-risk subset of schools in Chile, Mexico, and Colombia (resilience defined as high community crime risk via C_COMCRI combined with low student-reported physical/verbal abuse via S_ABUSE). At the school level, student and school questionnaire variables were aggregated (means) and analyzed with CART to rank predictors by normalized importance (threshold ≥40%), followed by country-specific logistic regression models using the selected predictor sets. Logistic regression model fit was moderate: Nagelkerke R2 was 0.46 for Chile (N=2581), 0.56 for Mexico (N=3488), and 0.34 for Colombia (N=3185). Across countries, the most consistent signals involved students’ civic attitudes/perceptions (e.g., interaction quality, empathy, gender equality, civic responsibility) rather than purely structural school factors. The paper acknowledges cross-sectional endogeneity/reverse causality risk, and it does not report a missing-data handling strategy, limiting interpretability of the observed associations.
